edition.deck: Ukraine’s war spills into the Baltic, climate talks remain deadlocked and a UK-EU reset faces a dispute over student fees. In Denmark, officials face scrutiny over flour recalls and rising school absence.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting from Saturday. Returning coverage is included only where the gather adds a meaningful update or distinct reporting; allegations and unresolved claims remain attributed.

content.headline: Zelensky calls Crimean Bridge strike a ‘fair response’ to Russian attacks
content.shortHeadline: Zelensky calls bridge strike a ‘fair response’
content.standfirst: Ukraine’s president says Russia has carried out 109 attacks on bridges in Ukraine. The latest strikes damaged the road link to occupied Crimea, while Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities continued.

image.caption: Wes Streeting meets Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv during a visit to show European support for Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelensky has called Ukraine’s strikes on the Crimean Bridge a “fair response” to what he said were 109 Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine. The strikes destroyed part of the bridge’s road section, leaving it unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks continued after the bridge strike. Local officials said a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old medic were killed in Kryvyi Rih, Zelensky’s home city, and 58 people were injured. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, visiting Kyiv, urged allies to do more to support Ukraine.

content.headline: COP31 talks remain deadlocked over fossil fuels and climate finance
content.shortHeadline: COP31 deadlock over fossil fuels and climate finance
content.standfirst: Negotiations in Turkey have run into Saturday, with countries divided over a draft that omits fossil fuels and weakens an electrification proposal. Developing countries are also pressing for more adaptation funding.

image.caption: Climate activists protest outside the COP31 plenary hall in Antalya.

sources.originalTitle: Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal
Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve

segments.body: COP31 negotiations have gone into overtime, with countries unable to agree on a final text. A draft released on Thursday removed a reference to moving away from fossil fuels, drawing opposition from countries including Panama, France and several other European and island states.

segments.title: A compromise still in question
segments.body: The dispute also reaches beyond fossil fuels: the draft makes a proposed global target for electricity use a voluntary option, while African negotiators say adaptation finance remains unresolved. China has endorsed the 2035 electrification goal with Australia, but a senior Chinese adviser told the Guardian that requiring the electricity to be clean would be harder to achieve.

perspectives.body: A senior Chinese government adviser backs electrification and says China will share its clean-technology experience, but cautions that requiring the target to be met entirely with low-carbon electricity would make it harder.

content.headline: Russian cargo ship hit by drones in Gulf of Finland, officials say
content.shortHeadline: Russian cargo ship damaged in Gulf of Finland drone strike
content.standfirst: The Sparta II was damaged and caught fire before drifting into Finnish waters, where its crew was being evacuated. Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the strike.

image.caption: The Sparta II cargo ship was damaged in a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland.

sources.originalTitle: What to know as Russian cargo ship ‘on fire after drone attack’ in the Baltic Sea
Fragtskib, der brænder i Østersøen, er kendt for at fragte våben for Rusland
Russisk fragtskib angrebet i Den Finske Bugt

segments.body: A drone strike damaged the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, according to Finnish and Russian officials. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish territorial waters. Authorities said the crew was being evacuated; the extent of the damage was still being assessed.

segments.title: A ship with reported military links
segments.body: Finnish officials said the vessel was linked to Russia’s armed forces, while a Finnish military spokesperson said Ukraine was likely behind the strike, according to Yle. Ukraine has not commented. The ship has been sanctioned by the US and is reported to have transported military equipment for Russia.

perspectives.body: A Danish Defence Academy analyst sees the strike as part of Ukraine’s widening campaign against Russian-linked shipping, while cautioning that Ukraine may keep such attacks close to Russia rather than carry them out in Danish waters.

content.headline: Mexican special forces arrest FBI-wanted cartel leader after shoot-out
content.shortHeadline: FBI-wanted Mexican cartel leader arrested after shoot-out
content.standfirst: Fausto Isidro “Chapo Isidro” Meza Flores was detained with a lieutenant in Sinaloa, Mexican officials say. The US is seeking his extradition over alleged drug trafficking and other crimes.

image.caption: Fausto Isidro “Chapo Isidro” Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday.

sources.originalTitle: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out

segments.body: Mexican special forces arrested Fausto Isidro “Chapo Isidro” Meza Flores and a lieutenant in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday, Mexico’s defence secretariat said. The authorities said troops came under fire and explosives before entering the property and detaining the two men.

Meza Flores, who was placed on the FBI’s most-wanted list in 2025, is accused by US authorities of trafficking drugs including fentanyl and cocaine. The US is seeking his extradition. He and his organisation are also accused of kidnapping, extortion and torture; the charges have not been adjudicated in this report.

content.headline: FBI investigating reported breach of US criminal information database
content.shortHeadline: FBI investigates reported hack of criminal database
content.standfirst: US media report that hackers may have breached the FBI’s National Crime Information Center, used by law enforcement for warrants and background checks. The bureau had not publicly confirmed the reported breach.

sources.originalTitle: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database

segments.body: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center database, US media reported, citing two people briefed on the issue. The system is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

The FBI had not responded to the BBC’s request for comment. Asked about the reported breach, President Donald Trump said he had “just heard” about it. The extent of any access to the database, and whether information was taken, was not established in the report.

content.headline: Nepal’s new prime minister faces a delicate India reset on first visit
content.shortHeadline: Nepal PM’s first India visit tests hopes for a reset
content.standfirst: Balendra Shah meets Narendra Modi on Sunday, with trade, energy and flood reconstruction expected on the agenda. A long-running border dispute and Nepal’s ties with China complicate the effort to improve relations.

image.caption: Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah arrives in Delhi for a two-day visit.

sources.originalTitle: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit

segments.body: Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah arrives in Delhi on Sunday for his first bilateral visit since his party came to power in March. Talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are expected to cover trade, energy cooperation, new air routes and assistance after August’s devastating floods.

segments.title: A relationship with unresolved strains
segments.body: India and Nepal share close ties and more than $9bn in annual trade, but the balance favours India and relations have been strained by territorial disputes and accusations of political interference. Shah’s recent party delegation to China also underscores Kathmandu’s effort to balance ties with its powerful neighbours.

content.headline: Anthropic mathematician claims AI helped prove the Riemann hypothesis
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic mathematician claims AI proof of Riemann hypothesis
content.standfirst: Levent Alpöge says he used a non-public version of Claude to produce a proof of the 170-year-old problem. Experts have yet to verify it, and the review may take months.

sources.originalTitle: In a year of AI solving maths problems, an Anthropic worker says he may have cracked the biggest

segments.body: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he used the company’s Claude chatbot over about six weeks to produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a famous, longstanding problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The proof is more than 250,000 pages long in the computer language Lean.

segments.title: Verification is the key test
segments.body: The claim remains unverified. Mathematician Terence Tao said the proof would take time to assess, while earlier AI-generated mathematical claims have also faced scrutiny. Alpöge said he used a non-public version of Claude.

perspectives.body: Terence Tao says reviewing the proof will take time, though the presence of a human author may help experts assess it—unlike some earlier AI-generated claims.

content.headline: China’s nuclear expansion raises concern over arms-race risks
content.shortHeadline: China’s nuclear buildup fuels concern over arms-race risks
content.standfirst: China’s arsenal has grown rapidly, according to US and independent estimates, while existing nuclear-control agreements have lapsed. Experts cited by the i Paper warn that uncertainty and short decision times raise the danger of miscalculation.

image.caption: Chinese liquid-fuelled intercontinental strategic missiles on display in Beijing in 2025.

sources.originalTitle: China’s ‘hot and heavy’ nuclear surge is worrying Trump, and rightly so

segments.body: China’s nuclear stockpile has expanded from about 200 warheads in 2019 to an estimated 600 last year, according to US and independent estimates cited by the i Paper. The article says it could reach 1,000 by 2030, still well below the estimated US and Russian stockpiles.

segments.title: Uncertainty and escalation
segments.body: Experts quoted by the i Paper warn that limited transparency about Beijing’s plans can encourage worst-case planning. One researcher also raised concern that a system designed to launch a counterstrike on warning could leave leaders only minutes to judge whether an alert is real. No new arms-control agreement appears imminent, the article says.

perspectives.body: Harvard researcher Hui Zhang argues Washington should pair pressure on Beijing with limits on its own missile-defence plans, which he says could otherwise intensify China’s incentive to launch on warning.

content.headline: UK-EU reset deals face dispute over student fees and implementation
content.shortHeadline: UK-EU reset deals face a student-fee dispute
content.standfirst: The package covers food trade, emissions and youth mobility, including a scheme for up to 100,000 young people. Ed Miliband says it will proceed without a tuition-fee agreement, but EU documents suggest implementation could be held up.

image.caption: Andy Burnham and EU leaders join hands after the UK-EU summit in Brussels.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit
Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK makes deals on trade and young people

segments.body: The UK and EU have agreed measures on food and drink standards, emissions trading and youth mobility. The scheme would allow up to 100,000 young people from each side to live, work, study and travel across the Channel. Andy Burnham says the package could boost UK GDP by £17bn a year; that is a government estimate.

segments.title: Different accounts of the condition
segments.body: Ed Miliband told the BBC the agreements will come into force even if the sides fail to agree on tuition fees for EU students. But the Guardian reports that an EU statement says the three agreements will not be adopted before a deal on equal treatment over fees. The issue is expected to be negotiated over the coming months.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that a confidential EU statement conditions adoption of the three agreements on the outcome of tuition-fee negotiations—at odds with Miliband’s assurance that they will proceed regardless.

content.headline: Doctor barred from treating patients also advised in parents’ neglect case
content.shortHeadline: Doctor barred from clinical work advised in parents’ case
content.standfirst: The Guardian reports that Prof Peter Hindmarsh wrote an expert report in a prosecution after his hospital had restricted his clinical work involving children with diabetes. The CPS says it met its disclosure obligations; the parents have applied to appeal.

image.caption: Prof Peter Hindmarsh, who provided expert evidence in the prosecution of Damion and Tamara Thomas.

sources.originalTitle: Letby trial doctor barred from treating patients was expert witness in another case

segments.body: Prof Peter Hindmarsh wrote an expert report for the prosecution of Damion and Tamara Thomas, who were convicted in the case of their son Joshua’s death from diabetic ketoacidosis. At the time, University College London Hospitals had excluded Hindmarsh from treating child patients with diabetes, citing safety concerns, the Guardian reports.

segments.title: Disclosure questions remain
segments.body: The Guardian says Hindmarsh did not disclose the hospital’s restrictions and related concerns to the police when he prepared his report; the CPS learned of the GMC investigation later. The CPS says it met its disclosure obligations and the police say they provided information in a timely manner. The Thomas family has applied for permission to appeal.

content.headline: NHS hospitals plan faster Alzheimer’s diagnosis using blood tests
content.shortHeadline: Hospitals prepare to bring Alzheimer’s blood tests into care
content.standfirst: Some hospitals plan to offer blood tests from early 2027, potentially shortening diagnosis from months or years to days. Trials assessing how the tests fit into NHS services are not due to finish until 2029.

image.caption: A blood sample is taken for testing.

sources.originalTitle: Blood tests that cut Alzheimer’s diagnosis from years to days coming in early 2027

segments.body: Blood tests that measure a form of tau protein may help identify Alzheimer’s disease and distinguish it from some other causes of memory problems. University College Hospital in London already offers the test, and Manchester Brain Health Centre says it plans to start in the coming weeks; more hospitals are expected to follow in 2027.

segments.title: Access and evidence still developing
segments.body: Two large trials are assessing how the tests should be used in NHS care and are due to finish in 2029. There is no central register of hospitals offering the service, raising the possibility of uneven access. Doctors caution that the blood test is used alongside clinical and cognitive assessment, not as a stand-alone diagnosis.

content.headline: Migrants say proposed UK settlement changes could reset years of residence
content.shortHeadline: Migrants say settlement changes could reset years of residence
content.standfirst: The government plans to scrap the 10-year Long Residence route to settlement, which currently counts time on student and graduate visas. People affected say years of lawful residence may no longer count; the start date has not been announced.

image.caption: Harry Mithun says a proposed change could undo years of planning towards UK settlement.

sources.originalTitle: Indefinite leave to remain changes are a betrayal – I’ve been here for nine years

segments.body: Harry Mithun, who moved to the UK from Sri Lanka in 2017, says he had planned to apply for indefinite leave to remain in 2027. Under proposed changes, the Long Residence route is to be scrapped and time on student or graduate visas will no longer count towards settlement, leaving him facing at least another decade before he can apply.

segments.title: Government says settlement must be earned
segments.body: Other people interviewed by the i Paper describe uncertainty over whether they can remain in the UK or make long-term plans. The Home Office says those who contribute most will qualify fastest and that people who do not follow the rules may wait longer or be refused. The changes’ start date has not been announced.

content.headline: Heavy rain warning for south-west England as cold snap gives way
content.shortHeadline: Heavy rain warning for south-west England on Sunday
content.standfirst: More than 100mm could fall on Dartmoor, the Met Office says, with flood alerts and possible travel disruption. The location of the heaviest rain remains uncertain.

image.caption: A road across Dartmoor, where the Met Office says more than 100mm of rain could fall.

sources.originalTitle: Cold gives way to rain in parts of UK as weather warning issued for south-west England

segments.body: A weather warning for heavy rain in Devon and Cornwall is in force from 6am on Sunday until midnight. The Met Office says 20–40mm is likely across much of the warning area, with 60–80mm possible in parts of south Devon and Cornwall and more than 100mm possible on Dartmoor.

Flooding and travel disruption are possible, and the Met Office warns of a risk of power cuts. Cold-health alerts remain in place in parts of northern England until Tuesday morning after temperatures fell to −10.6C at Tulloch Bridge in the Highlands. Forecasters say the exact path of the heaviest rain is uncertain.

content.headline: Forecast energy-bill rise could add more than £400 to annual costs
content.shortHeadline: Forecast energy-bill rise could add £443 to annual costs
content.standfirst: Cornwall Insight forecasts a 26% increase in the price cap from January, taking a typical bill to about £2,166 a year. Ofgem will announce the confirmed cap on 25 November.

image.caption: Elaine says energy costs have led her to use her oven only rarely.

sources.originalTitle: I’m 77, live alone and can’t afford to use my oven – how am I supposed to live?

segments.body: Cornwall Insight forecasts that Ofgem’s energy price cap could rise by 26% on 1 January, adding £443 to the annual bill for a typical household and taking it to £2,166. The forecast is not the final price-cap decision; Ofgem is due to announce the January-to-March level on 25 November.

People interviewed by the i Paper describe limiting heating and cooking because of current costs. The government says it has taken action to give households “breathing space” and maintains its commitment to lower bills by up to £300 by 2030. Cornwall Insight’s forecast does not include the government’s one-off £100 payment for eligible homes in England.

content.headline: Peter Fluck, Spitting Image caricaturist, dies aged 85
content.shortHeadline: Spitting Image caricaturist Peter Fluck dies aged 85
content.standfirst: Fluck and co-creator Roger Law made 18 seasons of the British satirical series, which ran from 1984 to 1996 and lampooned public figures in Britain and around the world.

image.caption: Peter Fluck and Roger Law with Spitting Image puppets in 1986.

sources.originalTitle: Peter Fluck, caricaturist behind Spitting Image, dies aged 85

segments.body: Artist Peter Fluck, who became known for co-creating the satirical television series Spitting Image with Roger Law, has died aged 85. The show ran for 18 seasons between 1984 and 1996, using puppets to satirise prominent figures. Fluck later moved to Cornwall and continued his artistic work.

content.headline: Danish parties back tougher line after alleged Russian-linked plot
content.shortHeadline: Broad backing for tougher response to alleged Russia-linked plot
content.standfirst: Two Danish men have been charged over an alleged plan to kill Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner. Opposition parties back proposed tougher penalties and restrictions on Russian visas; the Russian embassy denies evidence of Moscow’s involvement.

image.caption: Denmark’s foreign and justice ministers announced measures after two men were charged in the alleged plot.

sources.originalTitle: Bred politisk opbakning til at stramme linjen over for Rusland og LTF
Ikke første gang LTF arbejder for udenlandske interesser

segments.body: Several Danish opposition parties have backed government proposals for tougher penalties for crimes carried out on behalf of others or a foreign state, and limits on non-essential visas for Russian citizens. The proposals follow charges against two Danish men accused of attempting a contract killing targeting Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner.

segments.title: Allegations and response
segments.body: The case concerns an alleged plot involving Russia’s FSB and members linked to the banned Loyal to Familia gang, according to reporting and investigators cited by TV 2. The Russian embassy says Denmark has presented no evidence of Russian involvement. The allegations have not been established at trial.

perspectives.body: A former PET operational chief describes the alleged use of Danish gang members by a foreign state as a step up in the threat, while a TV 2 crime presenter says links between criminal groups and foreign interests have arisen before.

content.headline: Food authority criticised for delay in recalling flour linked to rodent-affected
content.shortHeadline: Food authority criticised over delayed flour recall
content.standfirst: TV 2 reports the Food Agency received a DTU assessment warning that a health risk could not be ruled out, but waited 50 days to seek its own assessment. Flour products have since been recalled; the actual risk remains uncertain.

image.caption: A nest made from dead mice at the Danish Agro warehouse linked to the grain used in recalled flour.

sources.originalTitle: Styrelse vidste, at mel kunne udgøre en sundhedsrisiko, men stoppede ikke salget

segments.body: The Danish Veterinary and Food Administration received a DTU Food Institute assessment on 15 September warning that processing might not have removed bacteria, viruses or toxins from grain stored at a rodent-affected site. TV 2 reports the agency waited 50 days before requesting its own assessment; products made with the grain were recalled this week.

segments.title: Agency and retailer questions
segments.body: Two food-law professors told TV 2 the agency should have acted sooner when the assessment raised doubt about its earlier decision. The agency’s director has called the initial decision wrong and regrettable. It remains unclear when shops stopped selling the products; the agency did not comment on the latest reporting.

content.headline: More than one in five Danish school pupils missed at least 20 days
content.shortHeadline: More than one in five pupils missed 20 school days
content.standfirst: New figures show average absence reached 7.6% in the 2025–26 school year, above the 5–6% recorded for much of the previous decade. A children’s charity is urging schools to identify problems earlier.

image.caption: VIVE analyst Mikkel Giver Kjer says the latest school-absence figures are deeply concerning.

sources.originalTitle: Det er "helt vildt”, siger ekspert om nye tal for skolefravær
Børns Vilkår ønsker tidligere indsats mod skolefravær

segments.body: More than one in five pupils in Denmark’s public schools missed at least 20 days in the 2025–26 school year, according to figures from the Ministry of Children and Education. Average absence was 15 days, or 7.6% of school days, compared with 5–6% for much of the period from 2010 to 2021.

segments.title: Calls for earlier help
segments.body: The children’s charity Børns Vilkår wants schools to improve attendance tracking so they can identify emerging patterns and support pupils before absences become entrenched. A national knowledge centre and new government measures are being introduced, but a researcher cited by TV 2 says more action may be needed.

perspectives.body: Børns Vilkår’s director argues that inconsistent absence records make it harder for schools to spot an emerging pattern and calls for a clear person responsible for helping each child return.

content.headline: Experts disagree over causes of Denmark’s persistent train delays
content.shortHeadline: Experts and minister disagree on why Danish trains keep failing
content.standfirst: DSB has not met its punctuality target this year, and experts point to ageing infrastructure and divided responsibilities. Transport Minister Karina Lorentzen Dehnhardt says extensive construction work and unexpected incidents are the main problems.

image.caption: Passengers wait at Ringsted Station during a period of train disruption.

sources.originalTitle: Togkaos, togkaos og mere togkaos: Her er eksperternes løsning

segments.body: DSB has failed to meet its punctuality target at any point this year, according to DR. Experts say delays and cancellations reflect several problems, including worn rails, signalling faults and the division of responsibilities between DSB, which runs trains, and Banedanmark, which manages the infrastructure.

segments.title: Different diagnoses
segments.body: Some experts argue the two organisations’ separate responsibilities make it harder to coordinate maintenance and operations; one suggests considering a single organisation. The transport minister disputes that collaboration is the current problem, pointing instead to major works across the network and unforeseen incidents. She says EU rules prevent a merger.

perspectives.body: Transport Minister Karina Lorentzen Dehnhardt rejects the view that poor cooperation is the main issue, saying the railway is a major construction site and unexpected events are disrupting services.

content.headline: Experts warn Pokémon card vending machines may normalise gambling-like habits
content.shortHeadline: Pokémon card machines spark concern over gambling-like play
content.standfirst: A Danish gambling researcher says the machines’ random rewards and instant purchase can resemble gambling, especially when placed in toy departments. Salling Group says buyers are guaranteed a card and rejects the comparison.

sources.originalTitle: Ny Pokémon-automat møder kritik

segments.body: Pokémon card vending machines in Bilka have drawn criticism from a customer who says their placement in a toy department and the chance to buy repeated random cards can expose children to gambling-like behaviour. A researcher at Aarhus University says random rewards can strongly encourage repeated use.

segments.title: The retailer’s defence
segments.body: Salling Group says the machines are a collectible product, not gambling, because every purchase delivers a card. A psychologist interviewed by TV 2 also says the machines cannot be directly linked to gambling addiction, while warning that their visibility may normalise spending in the hope of a valuable reward.

content.headline: Pilot social ambulance finds residents missing from support services
content.shortHeadline: Pilot social ambulance reaches residents unknown to services
content.standfirst: A six-month pilot in five municipalities in Region Zealand recorded 300 tasks and 164 contacts with residents. The service pairs social workers with ambulance staff to find people who may not seek help themselves.

image.caption: Social worker Katrine G. Jensen and ambulance worker Glenn Winge carry out outreach in Region Zealand.

sources.originalTitle: Katrine forlod skrivebordet og fandt mennesker, kommunen ikke anede fandtes

segments.body: A social ambulance pilot in five municipalities in Region Zealand has recorded 300 tasks and 164 contacts during its first six months. Social worker Katrine G. Jensen and ambulance staff visit places where residents in difficult circumstances may gather, aiming to connect people with support they have not sought themselves.

The pilot differs from the permanent Copenhagen service because residents in rural areas may be less visible and often need someone to alert the team. The project is funded through the end of 2027; staff say six months is too short to establish its longer-term effect.

content.headline: Nearly one in three young Danes has private pension savings, survey finds
content.shortHeadline: Nearly one in three young Danes has private pension savings
content.standfirst: A YouGov survey for Nordea found that almost a third of 18- to 29-year-olds have opened a pension account outside an employer scheme. Experts say it may offer flexibility, but money can be locked away for decades.

image.caption: An illustration accompanying DR’s report on young people’s private pension savings.

sources.originalTitle: Privat pensionsopsparing hitter blandt unge - eksperter svarer på, om det er en god ide

segments.body: Almost one in three Danes aged 18 to 29 has a private pension savings account outside an employer’s scheme, according to a YouGov survey for Nordea. A Nordea personal-finance expert sees the result as a sign of interest in personal finances; a CBS professor says the figure sounds high and notes many young people lack workplace pensions.

Experts say a separate account may offer different investment options or flexibility for people hoping to retire early, but may be unnecessary for someone already covered by an employer scheme. Contributions can also be difficult or costly to access before retirement, potentially decades away.

content.headline: Peter Gabriel’s new album opens into a world of ideas
content.shortHeadline: Peter Gabriel’s album opens into a world of ideas
content.standfirst: The rock innovator discusses his sprawling new record, artificial intelligence and the science that fascinates him. His digressions—from bonobos to brain-computer interfaces—are part of a creative life that resists the album-tour-album treadmill.

image.caption: Peter Gabriel.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel

segments.body: Peter Gabriel’s new album, o\i, runs nearly 90 minutes across 13 tracks and comes in two mixes. But a conversation about the record quickly expands into his interests in science, consciousness, communication between species and artificial intelligence. At 76, he says the diversions are part of what feeds his music.

segments.title: Curiosity as a creative method
segments.body: Gabriel sees AI as both a source of danger and a possible creative tool. He warns that its use in warfare is frightening and calls for international agreements and safeguards, while arguing that it could help people explore making music, films and art. He also imagines future work involving brain-computer interfaces, though some of his ideas remain sketches rather than finished projects.

content.headline: Fontaines DC turn arena-sized gloom into a communal thrill
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines DC make arena-sized gloom feel communal
content.standfirst: At Liverpool’s M&S Bank Arena, the Irish band’s bleak songs became huge singalongs. A set weighted towards their latest album showed how confidently they have moved from Dublin clubs to the biggest stages.

image.caption: Grian Chatten performing with Fontaines DC at Liverpool’s M&S Bank Arena.

sources.originalTitle: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness

segments.body: Fontaines DC arrived in Liverpool having made the leap from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums ahead. Grian Chatten entered partway through the opening song, then worked the crowd with a confidence the review says was less apparent on smaller stages. Their dark songs—about depression and modern malaise—took on an anthemic, celebratory force in the room.

segments.title: A set built for the bigger room
segments.body: Nine songs came from the band’s latest album, Dopamine Chamber, while only one remained from each of the first two records. New songs including “Marianne” and “Mimesis” already sounded like crowd favourites; the audience supplied Rosalía’s part on “Where Is Gone?” The review calls the show another triumph for a band whose rapid ascent has so far seemed effortless.

content.headline: Armand Hammer turn fractured rap into urgent political art
content.shortHeadline: Armand Hammer make urgent art from fractured rap
content.standfirst: On Snakes & Ladders, billy woods and Elucid pair intricate writing with beats from a community of collaborators. The review hears a demanding record that connects private unease to a wider history of oppression.

sources.originalTitle: Snakes & Ladders

segments.body: The New York duo Armand Hammer—billy woods and Elucid—build Snakes & Ladders from fragmented observations, sharp wordplay and production by a wide circle of artists associated with their label, Backwoodz Studioz. The review finds a coherent, uneasy whole in the range of sounds, from spare piano to reverberant percussion and acid-jazz textures.

segments.title: Language as cultural work
segments.body: The review places the album within a longer tradition of Black political art, linking its accounts of daily life to colonialism, power and the present political climate. It argues that the record’s difficulty is part of its purpose: the duo’s writing is not designed to offer easy answers, but to make the search for meaning and solidarity feel necessary.

content.headline: Stella Z turns field recordings into a dreamlike ambient world
content.shortHeadline: Stella Z builds a dreamlike world from field recordings
content.standfirst: Sounds gathered on trips to China shape Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, a nocturnal collage of whispers, percussion and electronics. Its drifting textures are most compelling when they make the listener feel unmoored.

image.caption: Stella Z.

sources.originalTitle: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming

segments.body: Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z draws on recordings made during visits to China, including the sounds of a pharmacy and the Fujian mountains at night. Across eight tracks, those fragments meet whispers, polyrhythmic percussion and electronics, creating music that moves between ambient, new age, downtempo, acid and dub.

The album’s dream imagery is clearest in pieces that blur voices and atmosphere: “Mira Miruna” gradually brings words out of a hazy arrangement, while “Exit, Elsewhere” layers narration and bells into disorientation. A remix by Valentina Magaletti can grate, but the record’s more awkward moments still conjure what the review calls invigorating visions of woozy wilderness.

content.headline: R.E.M.’s Reveal reissue makes a case for its lasting influence
content.shortHeadline: R.E.M.’s Reveal looks newly influential on reissue
content.standfirst: The 25th-anniversary edition revisits a dreamy, synth-and-strings pivot made after Bill Berry left the band. The review hears an album that now looks like an overlooked link to 21st-century indie-pop.

sources.originalTitle: Reveal (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Released in 2001, Reveal found R.E.M. working as a trio with additional musicians after drummer Bill Berry’s retirement. Its warm electronic and orchestral textures marked a gentler, more ruminative turn. The reissue adds live material from a European promotional performance, where the expanded group reshapes both newer songs and older favourites.

segments.title: A record heard in a new light
segments.body: The review argues that Reveal’s once-misty folk-rock now sounds like a touchstone for indie-pop, anticipating later artists who drew on trip-hop, sample-pop and electronic music. “Imitation of Life” and “All the Way to Reno” stand out, while the reissue’s live set shows the band enjoying its reinvention rather than trying to recreate its earlier sound.

content.headline: Thoom fuses hyperpop and Arabic instrumentation into a vivid debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom fuses hyperpop and Arabic sounds on her debut
content.standfirst: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, Beirut-born, Los Angeles-based artist Zeynab Marwan joins Arabic instrumentation to hyperpop’s digital intensity. The album’s most affecting moments make its emotional stakes feel as large as its sound.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: As Thoom, Zeynab Marwan brings hyperpop production together with Arabic instrumentation on her debut album. The review hears a striking fit between hard-edged club sounds and her voice, which can turn from fluid melody to a menacing, direct delivery. Producers Dylan Brady and Ike Clateman help build tracks that swing between aggressive and vulnerable.

segments.title: A question of belonging
segments.body: The closing song, “I’m Going Back to Lebanon,” makes the record’s most personal tension explicit: it is both a farewell to a lover and a longing to return to Marwan’s homeland, with no certainty that return is possible. The review sees that uncertainty as the clearest expression of the album’s emotional and political weight.

content.headline: Kim Deal’s Barbican concert gives her songs orchestral warmth
content.shortHeadline: Kim Deal’s Barbican set gives her songs orchestral warmth
content.standfirst: A 13-piece orchestra and choir expand songs from the Breeders and Deal’s solo work on Live at the Barbican. The performance is not a radical reinvention, but the arrangements and Deal’s vivid voice give it a character of its own.

sources.originalTitle: Live at the Barbican

segments.body: Kim Deal’s live album and concert film bring her regular band together with an orchestra and choir at London’s Barbican. Much of the set draws on her solo album Nobody Loves You More, with several earlier solo songs and Breeders material. The arrangements mostly stay close to the studio versions, but the strings and brass lend them a new warmth.

The review singles out the cello in “Beautiful Moon” and the fuller treatment of “Off You” as moments when the concert meaningfully changes the songs. Deal’s gravelly, expressive voice remains the centre of attention, especially on “Walking With a Killer”. The result is affectionate and substantial, even if it does not remake the live-album canon.

content.headline: Glastonbury’s 2027 headliners prompt a debate about ambition
content.shortHeadline: Do Glastonbury’s 2027 headliners lack ambition?
content.standfirst: An opinion piece argues that Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender are strong acts but too similar in career stage and audience to make an event-defining trio. It also points to festival fees and artists’ competing priorities.

image.caption: Harry Styles, one of Glastonbury’s announced 2027 Pyramid Stage headliners.

sources.originalTitle: Why Glastonbury can’t get good headliners

segments.body: Glastonbury’s announced 2027 Pyramid Stage headliners—Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender—have each earned a place at the top of the bill, the i Paper argues. Its criticism is that together they do not offer enough contrast or surprise, particularly when the festival has previously paired pop stars with established legends and acts from different parts of music.

segments.title: The economics of the booking
segments.body: The commentary suggests Glastonbury’s reported maximum headline fee of £500,000 may help explain why some major acts choose to tour elsewhere. It also argues that the festival’s cultural pull may have weakened as rock has lost ground and global pop stars have more options. This is the writer’s assessment, not a reported explanation from the festival or the acts.

content.headline: Police investigate allegations against Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq
content.shortHeadline: Depardieu and Houellebecq face a new police investigation
content.standfirst: French police are investigating a woman’s allegation that the actor and author assaulted and raped her during a 2018 film shoot. The reported complaint is under investigation; the claims have not been established in court.

image.caption: Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq.

sources.originalTitle: Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq investigated over on-set rape and assault allegations

segments.body: French police are investigating allegations that Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq assaulted and gang-raped a woman during filming of Thalasso in December 2018, according to sources cited by Agence France-Presse. Mediapart reported that the woman, identified by the pseudonym Alexandra, filed a complaint in 2025 and described being pinned down during a scene.

segments.title: Responses and separate proceedings
segments.body: Director Guillaume Nicloux told Mediapart he had not noticed any constraint during filming but had apologised to Alexandra. Her lawyers and representatives for Depardieu and Houellebecq did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment. Depardieu has separately dropped an appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on another film set; the allegations in the new investigation concern a different incident.

content.headline: A new documentary revisits the televangelists who reshaped US politics
content.shortHeadline: The televangelists whose scandals reshaped US politics
content.standfirst: Primetime Preacher$ traces the rise of Jerry Falwell, Jimmy Swaggart and Jim Bakker, linking church television, personal scandal and the growth of the religious right. Director Joe Berlinger says the story reaches beyond the pulpit into politics.

image.caption: Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker in 1986.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism

segments.body: Joe Berlinger’s Netflix documentary Primetime Preacher$ follows three influential US televangelists: Jerry Falwell, Jimmy Swaggart and Jim Bakker. It examines how television ministries and the prosperity gospel attracted large audiences and donations, while reporting on the scandals and financial improprieties that damaged their public standing.

segments.title: A political legacy
segments.body: Berlinger describes the televangelism boom as part of the rise of the religious right, a movement that became a powerful Republican constituency. The documentary also gives space to Tammy Faye Bakker’s more inclusive approach to faith and LGBTQ+ people, a contrast to the ambitions and controversies surrounding the ministry leaders.

perspectives.body: Berlinger says he began the film expecting a break from true crime, but came to see televangelism’s history as a story about the political influence of the religious right.

content.headline: Three critics debate the slippery ethics of You Can See Everything
content.shortHeadline: You Can See Everything: a gripping film that unsettles truth
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes has drawn sharply different responses. One review celebrates its audacious form; others warn that its focus on feeling and performance risks obscuring evidence and the harm caused by Theranos.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
Elizabeth Holmes is not the villain of You Can See Everything. That’s a problem

segments.body: You Can See Everything gives Nathan Fielder intimate access to Elizabeth Holmes shortly before she began serving her prison sentence for fraud. The film asks whether she believes her own claims, then makes a striking turn into reenactment with Amanda Seyfried. The Guardian review calls it a gripping, reckless high-wire act, while another review sees its refusal to examine the case evidence as a troubling choice.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s critical response argues that the film substitutes an extended test of Holmes’s sincerity for scrutiny of the evidence behind her conviction, risking a false equivalence between emotional impression and objective fact.

segments.body: The i Paper review also praises the film’s unusual form but questions whether its close attention to Holmes makes her seem too sympathetic. Its account of the film’s second half puts more emphasis on her husband, Billy Evans, and the possibility that his behaviour shifts the story’s focus away from Holmes. Together, the reviews show why the film’s formal audacity is also the source of its ethical unease.

content.headline: Robert Pattinson’s Bond casting raises questions for Batman’s future
content.shortHeadline: Pattinson’s Bond role puts Batman’s future in doubt
content.standfirst: With Robert Pattinson announced as the next James Bond, delays to The Batman: Part II have reportedly freed him from a third-film commitment. A separate change of director and new leadership at DC add uncertainty to the franchise’s future.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson as Batman.

sources.originalTitle: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast

segments.body: Robert Pattinson’s appointment as 007 arrives as The Batman: Part II faces delays and a reported change in its production team. According to the Wrap, the delay has freed Pattinson from his obligation to make a third Batman film, although he could still agree to return. The Guardian argues that DC should move quickly to secure him.

segments.title: Two franchises, different demands
segments.body: The piece says Matt Reeves remains committed to the sequel after stepping away from principal photography for a family matter, with Steven Soderbergh brought in to complete filming. Warner Bros’ takeover and new leadership at DC Studios add another unknown: whether the studio will retain the plan for a separate Batman within its shared superhero universe. Pattinson’s interest in carrying both roles is also unresolved.

content.headline: How should the next James Bond return after No Time to Die?
content.shortHeadline: How can the next James Bond return after his apparent death?
content.standfirst: Writers and producers offer competing ideas for restarting 007 after Daniel Craig’s final film appeared to kill him: explain a survival, reset continuity or simply introduce a new Bond without comment. The debate also revives questions about the character’s history.

image.caption: A Bond silhouette at the London premiere of No Time to Die.

sources.originalTitle: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?
The big problem with Robert Pattinson playing Bond

segments.body: No Time to Die ended with Bond apparently killed, but its closing promise that “James Bond will return” leaves the next film with a problem. The Guardian canvassed writers and producers on how a new instalment might proceed. Their options range from a story in which Bond survived to a clean reset that makes no attempt to explain the change.

perspectives.body: Russell T Davies argues that continuity has gone too far to resolve neatly: his suggestion is to recast the supporting roles too and let Robert Pattinson begin his first day as Bond without further explanation.

segments.body: The i Paper’s assessment of Pattinson’s casting raises a separate concern: he is already a major star with experience in several franchises, unlike the less established actors the Bond series has often chosen. That review questions whether the role will limit his range, while the Guardian’s respondents focus on how to move the character’s story forward.

content.headline: Brad Pitt’s Cliff Booth spin-off is a laid-back, macho detour
content.shortHeadline: Brad Pitt’s Cliff Booth spin-off coasts on charm
content.standfirst: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script for a 1970s-set return to the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood character. The BBC review enjoys the vintage Los Angeles detail but finds too little story or ambition beneath the nostalgia.

sources.originalTitle: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review: Brad Pitt returns to his Oscar-winning role in a 'macho fantasy' ★★★☆☆

segments.body: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth brings Brad Pitt back as the stuntman from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, in a film scripted by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher. Set in Los Angeles in 1977, it follows Cliff through a week of loose encounters before a pair of hitmen draw him into a job.

The BBC review enjoys the period details and Pitt’s easy charm, but says the film takes too long to reach its central predicament and offers little beyond a string of anecdotes. It also criticises the film’s narrow focus on straight, white men, calling the result a mellow, old-fashioned macho fantasy rather than the ambitious work the filmmakers’ reputations might suggest.

content.headline: Wicker’s strange romance asks what women want from a partner
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s wicker husband turns romance into a debate
content.standfirst: A village outsider pays for a husband made of willow in this bawdy fantasy starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård. A review enjoys its absurd comedy but questions its one-sided fantasy; the filmmakers and commentators connect it to domestic labour and desire.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it
A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a basketmaker to make her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård. The i Paper review calls the result hilarious and deliberately sexist: its wooden husband exists to please his wife, with little attention to his own agency. The piece enjoys the comedy while questioning what the fantasy implies.

segments.title: The appeal of an attentive partner
segments.body: The film’s co-director Eleanor Wilson says the story’s domestic dynamics feel especially current now that more people have language for the mental load of household work. Other commentators interviewed by the BBC connect the film to monster romances, outsider characters and the appeal of a partner who is kind and helpful without demanding praise.

perspectives.body: The filmmakers say the Wicker Husband’s appeal is not just his appearance: he notices what needs doing and acts without being asked. They link that detail to contemporary conversations about unequal domestic labour.

content.headline: This week’s cinema releases range from Theranos to a Hunger Games prequel
content.shortHeadline: The week’s cinema releases: from Theranos to Hunger Games
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s round-up spans Nathan Fielder’s close study of Elizabeth Holmes, a new Hunger Games prequel and films about Heysel, Gaza and the 1986 World Cup. Its brief verdicts also flag several films that reviewers find disappointing.

image.caption: A selection of films reviewed in the week’s UK cinema releases.

sources.originalTitle: Hungry for action? Our critics’ verdicts on the week’s UK cinema releases

segments.body: The week’s UK cinema list includes You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film about Elizabeth Holmes; Sunrise on the Reaping, a second Hunger Games prequel; and films revisiting the Heysel stadium disaster and the “hand of God” World Cup match. It also covers a Gaza hospital documentary and a film about a golf course in water-deprived Manila.

The round-up’s short reviews are far from uniformly enthusiastic: Peter Bradshaw calls the Hunger Games prequel a cash-grab, while the Gaza documentary is described by Cath Clarke as a powerful film driven by anger and despair. It offers a quick guide to a crowded release week rather than a single consensus verdict.

content.headline: Australian TV has found a global audience without sanding off its edges
content.shortHeadline: Australian TV is travelling the world on its own terms
content.standfirst: From Bluey to Colin from Accounts, Australian shows are reaching viewers far beyond home. Industry voices point to international funding, shifting commissioning habits and a willingness to trust audiences with locally specific stories.

image.caption: A selection of Australian television shows, including Bluey and Colin from Accounts.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s peak Aussie – and it’s fantastic!’ How Australian TV conquered the world

segments.body: Australian television has travelled widely in recent years, from children’s animation Bluey to comedy, crime drama and period series. Producers and broadcasters interviewed by the Guardian describe a change that accelerated around 2020, as international streamers funded local productions and overseas buyers began seeking shows from beyond the US and UK.

segments.title: Specificity travels
segments.body: Industry figures cite several factors, including remote collaboration, more international viewing and production budgets that can make Australian co-productions attractive. They also argue that shows need not explain every local expression or cultural reference: distinctive humour and perspective can be part of the appeal. The article stresses that Australia has a long storytelling history, even if international buyers are now paying closer attention.

perspectives.body: Several Australian creators reject the idea that their television has only recently become good. They say the difference is that international buyers have become more willing to recognise the distinctiveness of stories already being made.

content.headline: The BBC is putting some Christmas TV on iPlayer earlier this year
content.shortHeadline: The BBC is releasing some Christmas shows early
content.standfirst: Festive specials will appear on iPlayer from 27 November, weeks before some television broadcasts. The BBC says earlier access reflects changing viewing habits; the Radio Times editor worries it could weaken the shared ritual of seasonal television.

image.caption: Mary Berry filming her Christmas Countdown.

sources.originalTitle: ‘In the office, there was a sharp intake of breath’: why has the BBC decided to celebrate Christmas earlier than ever?

segments.body: The BBC plans to make a selection of Christmas programmes available on iPlayer from 27 November, in some cases up to a month before their television broadcasts. The move follows the BBC’s analysis of increased viewing of festive shows ahead of Christmas and a drop-off in interest after 28 December.

segments.title: A different kind of Christmas schedule
segments.body: BBC iPlayer and TV channels director Dan McGolpin says an earlier release gives viewers a wider window and better value from programmes. Radio Times editor Shem Law accepts that broadcasters must respond to changing habits, but says early streaming could diminish the occasion of watching a Christmas special together. Major titles such as the Strictly special and the new Call the Midwife prequel remain scheduled for television first.

perspectives.body: Shem Law argues that advance streaming changes the shared experience of the Christmas TV schedule: family members may find that others have already watched the programmes chosen for a communal viewing.

content.headline: Blade Runner 2099’s atmosphere overwhelms its story
content.shortHeadline: Blade Runner 2099 is atmospheric but hard to follow
content.standfirst: The Guardian review admires the series’ industrial visuals and eerie sound, but says its slow pace and obscure plot make four hours hard to follow. Its central question is whether this world gains anything from being extended into television.

image.caption: Hunter Schafer as Cora and Michelle Yeoh as Olwen in Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099: fans will have no idea what is happening in this sci-fi sequel. Why is it even on TV?

segments.body: Set decades after Blade Runner 2049, the Prime Video series imagines a changed order in which replicants hunt humans. Hunter Schafer plays Cora, a human who infiltrates the police, while Michelle Yeoh plays a replicant near the end of her lifespan. The Guardian review says the show sustains the films’ bleak, oppressive atmosphere.

The review’s main objection is that mood takes precedence over clarity. It finds the plot difficult to follow, the dialogue sparse and the pacing slow, leaving the series’ themes of grief and isolation more exhausting than illuminating. The critic questions whether this kind of cinematic world benefits from being extended across television episodes.

content.headline: Melania’s two-part documentary is criticised as an extended advert
content.shortHeadline: Melania’s TV documentary leaves its reviewer cold
content.standfirst: A Guardian review finds little substance in the first lady’s two-part series, describing its short episodes as empty and self-promotional. It notes one brief shift towards the people affected by storms before the focus turns back to Melania Trump.

image.caption: Melania Trump.

sources.originalTitle: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space

segments.body: The Guardian review describes Melania as two episodes made up of short fragments, with little sense of a developed documentary series. It criticises Melania Trump’s flat delivery and says the programme’s polished, faux-home-video look does not give the material much substance.

The review identifies one moment when the series becomes more human: Melania meets people affected by Hurricane Helene and wildfires. But it says the sequence soon redirects attention to her own initiatives and website, leaving the critic to conclude that the programme functions more as promotion than as an examination of its subject.

content.headline: Bill’s Included wins praise for Rob Brydon but divides critics on its sitcom
content.shortHeadline: Bill’s Included: Rob Brydon shines, but do the characters?
content.standfirst: Two reviews agree that Rob Brydon is the sitcom’s chief asset but differ on whether his performance can carry it. One finds warmth and flashes of wit; the other says the supporting cast and storylines are too thin.

image.caption: Rob Brydon in Bill’s Included.

sources.originalTitle: Bill’s Included review – Rob Brydon’s new character is as glorious as Gavin & Stacey’s Uncle Bryn
Rob Brydon can do better than Bill’s Included

segments.body: Rob Brydon plays Bill, a divorced landlord who rents rooms to students and tries to become their friend. The Guardian review praises Brydon’s comic performance and sees a sweet, traditional sitcom with flashes of sharpness, but says the student characters and storylines are thin.

perspectives.body: The i Paper review is more dismissive: it finds Bill himself too unremarkable to make his ordinariness funny and argues that the role wastes Brydon’s comic range.

segments.body: Both critics compare the new character with Brydon’s Uncle Bryn from Gavin & Stacey, but reach different conclusions about the resemblance. The Guardian sees a similarly excruciating, endearing figure; the i Paper says the new role lacks the specificity that made Bryn memorable. Their shared concern is whether the show gives its other characters enough depth.

content.headline: Danny Robins explores belief and fear in The Witch Farm
content.shortHeadline: Danny Robins brings The Witch Farm to television
content.standfirst: The Uncanny host adapts his podcast about a reported haunting in rural Wales into a BBC drama. He says the story should leave room for scepticism as well as belief, and discusses how his own fear of death shapes his interest in the paranormal.

image.caption: Danny Robins, host of Uncanny and writer of The Witch Farm.

sources.originalTitle: Danny Robins: ‘My wife has never listened to Uncanny. She finds it terrifying’

segments.body: The Witch Farm adapts Danny Robins’s podcast about the Rich family’s reported experiences at a Welsh farmhouse between 1989 and 1996. The drama follows Bill, Liz and Bill’s teenage son as unsettling events make them question whether they are alone in their new home. Robins says he based the podcast on extensive conversations with Liz Rich.

segments.title: Keeping room for doubt
segments.body: Robins says he is not a believer in the supernatural, but remains open to what he cannot explain. He argues that stories should not simply declare ghosts real or validate every experience without question. His own panic attack and lasting fear of death, he says, helped him understand why people want to believe that life may continue beyond it.

content.headline: Open Secret revisits how Russell Brand’s behaviour was enabled
content.shortHeadline: Open Secret asks how Russell Brand’s behaviour went unchecked
content.standfirst: The Netflix documentary brings together testimony, journalism and archival footage about Russell Brand’s rise and abuse allegations. The review argues that its most disturbing point is how behaviour now seen in a different light was once tolerated by media and entertainment institutions.

image.caption: The documentary examines Russell Brand’s rise to fame and his subsequent fall.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Russell Brand documentary feels like a horror film

segments.body: Open Secret follows reporting by Sunday Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace and includes interviews with comedians, writers and former partners. The i Paper review considers how footage of Brand’s public persona and accounts from women sit alongside his recent conviction for rape and sexual assault.

segments.title: An industry’s blind spots
segments.body: The review argues that the documentary’s force lies not only in testimony about alleged abuse, but in its picture of the culture that enabled Brand. It points to the way his provocative public image and jokes were treated as entertainment while people who wanted to speak about their experiences feared they would not be believed.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans asking for a return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its latest hiatus
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, and a planned Christmas special was cancelled while the show has no current Doctor. Fans and former contributors disagree on why the latest run faltered, but hope the long-running series will return.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its 2025 series, and the BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+. A planned Christmas special was cancelled, with no current Doctor in place, while the corporation seeks a new partner to help fund future production. No replacement has yet been announced.

segments.title: What the show needs next
segments.body: The article weighs possible causes of the show’s recent difficulties, including scripts, casting and the failed hopes for the Disney+ partnership. Fan Frank Skinner says he is not sure the series needed a large investment to tell good stories and wants it back on screen. Former writer Nina Metivier points to its enduring values of kindness and curiosity.

content.headline: GTA VI makes its criminal chaos feel surprisingly intimate
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI turns criminal chaos into a love story
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s vast, filthy Florida-inspired world offers a startling range of things to do, but its emotional centre is the fugitive couple Jason and Lucia. The review finds new empathy alongside the series’ trademark excess.

image.caption: Jason and Lucia, the central couple in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto VI builds an enormous, intricately detailed world called Leonida, where players can rob banks, go to the gym, shop or simply explore. The Guardian reviewer spent 70 hours with the game and says its scope makes it difficult to define: it can feel like a crime film, a city simulator or an expansive life sim with criminals at its centre.

segments.title: A bond amid the mayhem
segments.body: The story follows Jason and Lucia, two fugitives trying to build a life together as they become entangled with criminals. After many hours in their company, the reviewer found their relationship unexpectedly moving. Their personalities are not blank stand-ins for the player, and small acts of kindness sit alongside the game’s extreme violence and vulgar humour.

segments.title: A world that can fight back
segments.body: The game’s detail can also make it frustrating: controls are complex, accidents can spiral and missions can fail for reasons that are not always clear. The review also notes that Lucia, the series’ first female protagonist, changes how its treatment of women lands, without making the case that the game is feminist. Its lewdness and violence remain central to the experience.

content.headline: Why Grand Theft Auto VI is unlikely to become a TV series
content.shortHeadline: Why GTA VI may work best as a game, not a TV show
content.standfirst: Take-Two’s chief says an adaptation would need to delight players, but a Guardian essay argues that the game’s defining freedom resists a linear version. Its scale and commercial success also give the company little reason to take the risk.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI, the game at the centre of the adaptation debate.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto would be a huge TV series – here’s why it will never happen

segments.body: Take-Two Interactive chief executive Strauss Zelnick has said a film or television adaptation of Grand Theft Auto would need to engage and delight the game’s audience, while acknowledging the risk of failure. The Guardian essay agrees that the bar is high, arguing that players’ open-ended choices are central to the experience.

A scripted series would have to turn a world in which players choose how to spend their time into a fixed narrative, the piece argues. It also points to the franchise’s enormous commercial success as a reason its owners may prefer not to risk a weaker adaptation. The essay compares GTA with other popular works whose creators have resisted screen versions.

content.headline: A veteran games player finds a role in an indie horror game
content.shortHeadline: After 50 years of gaming, he’s starring in one
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s games writer describes voicing Draga, the lead character in the independent survival-horror game Black Tides Draga’s Wake. The experience has changed how he thinks about voice acting and the people who make games.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist of Black Tides Draga’s Wake, voiced by the writer.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: After decades of playing games, the Guardian writer was asked to voice Draga, a sailor in the survival-horror game Black Tides Draga’s Wake. The project is being made by a distributed team working in their spare time, led by character artist Greg Strangis, whose previous credits include work for major studios.

segments.title: Finding the voice
segments.body: The writer initially disliked hearing his own voice on the game’s tough protagonist, then adjusted his delivery with Strangis’s direction. Recording improvised fight sounds in a garage was among the stranger tasks. The experience has also made him more aware of the performance and direction behind game characters—and gave his children a surprise when they recognised their father on screen.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans grieving a lost future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure means no new Mass Effect from the studio
content.standfirst: The Guardian writer reflects on EA’s closure of BioWare and cancellation of its next Mass Effect game. A personal account of the original trilogy explains why its character-driven choices and relationships remain so influential.

image.caption: Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s original trilogy.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The Guardian writer says EA has closed BioWare, cancelled its forthcoming Mass Effect game and left more than 400 people facing job losses. The piece connects the decision to EA’s debt and the studio’s failure to produce a critical or commercial hit in more than a decade, while mourning what the cancelled game might have been.

segments.title: The choices that stayed with players
segments.body: The writer recalls how the original trilogy made decisions feel personal: players shaped Commander Shepard’s identity, relationships with companions and the fate of species across the galaxy. The account argues that BioWare’s character-led, choice-driven storytelling helped set a standard for action role-playing games, making the studio’s loss feel larger than the cancellation of one sequel.

content.headline: Pancreatic cancer pill shrank tumours in a trial, but a cure is unproven
content.shortHeadline: Pancreatic cancer pill shows promise, but a cure is unproven
content.standfirst: In a trial of 61 people with advanced pancreatic cancer, daraxonrasib stopped tumours growing in most participants and made them undetectable on scans for some. Longer follow-up is needed to learn how durable the results are.

sources.originalTitle: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’

segments.body: In a trial involving 61 people with advanced pancreatic cancer, the KRAS inhibitor daraxonrasib stopped tumours growing in 90% of participants. Tumours shrank or disappeared in just over 60%, and became undetectable on CT scans in about 8%. After a year, 76.6% of participants were alive; the article reports that 40–45% of patients given chemotherapy alone usually survive a year.

segments.title: What the results cannot yet show
segments.body: Participants were followed for an average of 18 months, and some had not seen their cancer return during that period. Doctors say the pill cannot yet be considered a cure; longer studies will be needed to establish whether the effect lasts or any cancers enter remission. The researchers hope the approach may also work against other cancers with similar mutations, but that possibility needs testing.

content.headline: BepiColombo reaches Mercury ahead of its planned orbit insertion
content.shortHeadline: BepiColombo reaches Mercury, with orbit insertion ahead
content.standfirst: After more than eight years in flight, the European-Japanese mission is preparing to enter orbit around Mercury. Its two spacecraft are expected to begin science operations next April, investigating the planet’s surface, interior and magnetic field.

image.caption: Artist’s impression of the two BepiColombo orbiters at Mercury.

sources.originalTitle: Spacecraft reaches Mercury on second-ever mission to enter its orbit

segments.body: BepiColombo has reached Mercury after a journey of more than eight years and six billion miles. The mission is due to fire its thrusters to enter orbit on Saturday; in December, its European and Japanese orbiters are expected to separate and manoeuvre into different polar orbits. Science operations are scheduled to start in April.

segments.title: Questions for the twin orbiters
segments.body: The European orbiter will map the planet’s surface and composition and study its unusually large core. The Japanese orbiter will measure Mercury’s magnetic field and its extremely thin sodium exosphere. Researchers hope the mission will help explain how the dense planet formed so close to the sun, and investigate ice in craters that remain permanently in shadow.

content.headline: Scientists send a one-word message through a wall using gravity
content.shortHeadline: A one-word message crosses a wall by gravity
content.standfirst: In a proof-of-concept experiment, researchers encoded “gravity” in the movement of an elevator counterweight and detected it through a brick wall. The method is far too slow to be practical, but ordinary materials cannot screen the signal.

image.caption: Researchers at the University of Queensland beside the elevator used in the experiment.

sources.originalTitle: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message

segments.body: Physicists at the University of Queensland moved a 1.8-tonne elevator counterweight between two floors to represent binary digits. A gravimeter in a nearby bathroom detected the resulting tiny changes in gravity through a brick wall, allowing the team to send the word “gravity”. At one bit per minute, the message took nearly an hour.

segments.title: A demonstration, not a communications system
segments.body: The researchers describe the approach as “practically unblockable” because ordinary material cannot screen out a gravitational signal. But the researchers say it is currently far from useful: co-author Matthew Davis noted that NASA’s Voyager 1 can communicate with Earth faster. More sensitive quantum sensors could, in theory, extend the range and speed, but those sensors remain under development.

content.headline: Potatoes grow in simulated lunar soil, but need added organic matter
content.shortHeadline: Potatoes grow in simulated moon soil with added compost
content.standfirst: Researchers grew small potatoes in engineered lunar-soil simulant, but the plants struggled without vermicompost. The experiment is a step towards studying food production beyond Earth, not evidence that crops are ready to grow on the moon.

image.caption: Potatoes grown in simulated lunar soil in an Oregon State University laboratory.

sources.originalTitle: Spuds in space: scientists say potatoes could be key food source for future moon base

segments.body: A team backed by NASA grew Modoc potatoes in engineered materials designed to mimic lunar regolith. The simulated soil lacks nitrogen, and plants grown in it without vermicompost produced almost no roots or tubers. With as little as 5% vermicompost, they grew some; at 30%, yield matched plants grown in Earth soil under the same conditions.

segments.title: A long way from lunar farming
segments.body: The harvested potatoes were small, grown in pots and used for laboratory analysis rather than tasted. Researchers also warn that lunar regolith’s heavy-metal content can be harmful to plants. The work explores a possible ingredient in future greenhouse systems; it does not show that crops can yet be grown safely or at useful scale on the moon.

content.headline: Study questions blanket advice on saturated fat for some women
content.shortHeadline: Study questions blanket saturated-fat advice for some women
content.standfirst: An analysis of data from 20,000 women found a link between saturated-fat intake and heart attacks only among those with a high genetic predisposition to raised cholesterol. The researchers say the finding needs confirmation and should not prompt people to change their diets.

image.caption: An illustration of fatty plaques in an artery.

sources.originalTitle: Three surprising cholesterol myths – and what they mean for your diet

segments.body: Researchers analysed diet and health data from about 20,000 women in the US Women’s Health Initiative, comparing outcomes with genetic predisposition to high cholesterol. Among the quarter with the highest predisposition, greater saturated-fat intake was associated with more heart attacks. The analysis found no such correlation in women with low or medium predisposition.

segments.title: Why the result is not new diet advice
segments.body: The study is the first of its kind, involved women only and needs to be confirmed in other groups. Its lead researcher, Shoa Clarke, cautions against drawing conclusions or changing diets on the basis of one analysis. The article also notes other potential health concerns associated with saturated fat and red meat, and says cholesterol is only one part of the heart-disease picture.

content.headline: UN talks on binding rules for autonomous weapons collapse
content.shortHeadline: UN talks on autonomous weapons rules end without a treaty path
content.standfirst: States failed to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons after week-long talks in Geneva. The outcome leaves work on international rules stalled, despite a majority of participating states backing a new legal instrument.

image.caption: Delegates at the UN Review Conference on Conventional Weapons in Geneva.

sources.originalTitle: International talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse

segments.body: A week of negotiations at the UN’s Certain Conventional Weapons convention ended without a mandate to negotiate a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons. Because the forum requires consensus among its 128 parties, delegates adopted a weaker proposal to “elaborate by consensus” an instrument that may carry no legal obligations.

segments.title: Disagreement over what comes next
segments.body: More than 100 states had pushed for new rules, while several military powers were reluctant to accept a binding protocol. Critics say existing humanitarian law is not enough to address the new challenges. Russia led objections to the mandate, while the United States and other countries also resisted a binding agreement. A bloc of seven states had called for negotiations to begin within a year.

content.headline: UK operation secures tens of thousands of commercial fridges from hackers
content.shortHeadline: UK operation secures commercial fridges from a cyber flaw
content.standfirst: Researchers, government agencies and businesses moved refrigeration controllers offline or patched them after a vulnerability was found. There is no sign it was exploited in the UK, but the equipment can control temperatures across large groups of fridges and freezers.

image.caption: A supermarket refrigeration unit affected by a temperature-control cyber incident in Europe.

sources.originalTitle: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation

segments.body: A largely behind-the-scenes operation secured tens of thousands of refrigeration devices at UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and other sites. After researchers found a vulnerability in widely used UK controllers, companies took some devices offline, removed internet connections or monitored temperatures manually. The BBC reports there is no sign of malicious activity on the affected controllers.

segments.title: A dispute about the risk
segments.body: Security researchers said the controllers’ weak-password problem resembled systems targeted in cyber-attacks elsewhere in Europe. Manufacturer Resource Data Management disputes how critical the vulnerability was, saying tests involved dismantling its hardware; it says it issued patches and contacted customers.
