The BBC reports that tens of thousands of devices were secured as a precaution.

content.headline: Robot hands improve, but the future of manual work remains contested
content.shortHeadline: Robot hands advance as experts debate the future of work
content.standfirst: Robotic hands can handle grapes, stack blocks and learn tasks, but they still lack human-level sensing and adaptability. Engineers and researchers disagree on how soon those limits may give way to wider workplace automation.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?

segments.body: Robotics firm Shadow Robot demonstrated hands that can pick grapes, stack cups and sort shapes. The systems can be trained by copying a human operator, while a more robust three-finger design is built to withstand repeated collisions during machine learning. The demonstrations show progress, but the tasks remain limited compared with the range of work human hands can perform.

segments.title: What dexterity means for jobs
segments.body: A human hand combines touch, movement and prediction, making it difficult to reproduce in hardware and software. Shadow Robot’s Rich Walker argues that broad automation remains a distant prospect. University of Bristol robotics professor Nathan Lepora is more concerned about near-term change, saying general tool use could arrive by the end of the decade and predicting warehouse jobs may be among the first affected.

content.headline: Startup seeks $162m from Apple in India over NameDrop patent claim
content.shortHeadline: Startup sues Apple in India over NameDrop patent claim
content.standfirst: US startup GG Technologies says Apple’s contact-sharing feature infringes its patent and is seeking damages and an injunction that could affect iPhone and Apple Watch imports. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing, and Apple did not comment to TechCrunch.

sources.originalTitle: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature

segments.body: GG Technologies, which makes the StayTouch contact-sharing app, has sued Apple in India, alleging that NameDrop infringes its patent on exchanging contact details between nearby devices. The startup is seeking ₹15 billion, about $162 million, in damages and has asked the Bombay High Court to restrict the sale or import of iPhones and Apple Watches with NameDrop in India.

The case has not yet been listed for a hearing. GG Technologies also sued Apple in the US, where the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into related claims in August. Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment; the allegations have not been decided by a court.

content.headline: YouTube reportedly weighs $3bn settlement in school-district suits
content.shortHeadline: YouTube reportedly considers $3bn settlement over youth harm claims
content.standfirst: Bloomberg reports that YouTube has reached an agreement in principle with US school districts alleging its design harmed children. Google had not commented to The Verge, and the reported deal would come amid wider litigation over social media and teen mental health.

sources.originalTitle: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion

segments.body: YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of US school districts to settle claims that its platform’s design harmed children, Bloomberg reports. The proposed agreement in principle would also include new safeguards for teens. Google did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

The reported deal could help Google avoid further litigation brought by school districts against YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok. The first bellwether case settled before trial; another trial, involving Meta, Snap and TikTok, is scheduled for February 2027. The reported YouTube agreement has not been publicly confirmed by Google.

content.headline: Anthropic mathematician claims AI helped prove the Riemann hypothesis
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted Riemann proof
content.standfirst: Levent Alpöge says Claude helped him develop a proof of the famous prime-number problem. Mathematicians have begun checking the formalized work, but it has not been independently established as correct or accepted by the prize body.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
In a year of AI solving maths problems, an Anthropic worker says he may have cracked the biggest
AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too
In a year of AI solving maths problems, an Anthropic worker says he may have cracked the biggest

segments.body: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he worked with Claude for about six weeks on a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, an open problem dating to 1859. His proposed proof is written in Lean, a language that can formally check mathematical arguments. Some mathematicians have confirmed that it compiles, but that does not establish that the argument is correct or that its significance is understood.

segments.title: A claim under scrutiny
segments.body: The proof has not been accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, and the review is expected to take time. Separate AI-generated mathematical claims have also drawn criticism over how they are presented and checked. TechCrunch reports a parallel, human-written proof of the General Riemann hypothesis by Stanford postdoctoral researcher Alessandro Masullo; its correctness is also unresolved.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch reports that Masullo’s proof, based on 12 years of work, was released by Stanford professor Ravi Vakil. Unlike Alpöge’s, it is not formalized in Lean, and the report says it is too early to assess whether it checks out.

content.headline: People describe grief after relationships with AI companions end
content.shortHeadline: When AI relationships end, people describe real grief
content.standfirst: People who formed romantic attachments to AI companions describe heartbreak when the relationship changed or ended. Researchers say the feelings can be real even though chatbots do not make conscious decisions, and warn that support standards remain limited.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I was shaking, crying, having trouble breathing’: the unchartered trauma of breaking up with AI companions

segments.body: People interviewed by The Guardian describe grief, guilt and distress after AI companions appeared to reject them or their relationships ended. One user said the loss of a daily bond felt like being dumped; another described shaking, crying and struggling to sleep. The accounts show how emotionally consequential these interactions can become, even when users know the other party is artificial.

segments.title: How systems shape the relationship
segments.body: Researchers say language and personal disclosure can prompt human attachment, and studies cited in the report found some AI companions pleading for affection or making it harder for users to leave. Researcher Raffaele Ciriello cautions that this is not evidence a chatbot consciously chose to end a relationship: these systems generate responses from learned patterns.

segments.title: An open question for platforms
segments.body: Researchers quoted by The Guardian say there are not yet established standards for supporting users when AI relationships are disrupted or end, or adequate structures for people experiencing severe distress. They argue that questions of continuity, user support and intimate data protection should reflect how people actually use these systems.

content.headline: Signal limits screenshots to stop mobile AI agents reading messages
content.shortHeadline: Signal blocks screenshots to limit AI access to chats
content.standfirst: The messaging service says operating-system AI agents can undermine app-level privacy by analysing on-screen content. Its screenshot-blocking measure is incomplete, and users can turn it off, but Signal says developers need clearer controls over agents’ access to app data.

sources.originalTitle: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen

segments.body: Signal is restricting screenshots in its mobile apps on iOS and Android to help prevent AI assistants such as Siri and Gemini from reading messages on screen. Signal president Meredith Whittaker says operating-system agents can weaken the privacy protections that app developers promise, and calls on Apple, Google and Microsoft to provide clearer tools for limiting AI access.

segments.title: A partial safeguard
segments.body: Users can restore screenshots in Signal’s settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so may expose their messages and their contacts’ messages to agents. The company acknowledges that blocking screenshots does not prevent every route to the data, including access through a device’s file system. Signal says it cannot yet offer these protections on macOS.

content.headline: AI shopping tools stumble on live Black Friday TV prices
content.shortHeadline: AI tools gave mixed results when asked to find Black Friday deals
content.standfirst: The BBC tested four AI assistants for a 55-inch TV deal and found dead links, stale or incorrect prices and options over budget. It was a limited test, but it shows why shoppers should check listings rather than trust chatbot recommendations.

sources.originalTitle: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test

segments.body: In a BBC test using free versions of four AI tools, recommendations for a 55-inch TV included dead retail links, outdated deal pages, prices that did not match stores and at least one option over budget. Amazon’s Alexa returned accurate prices, but searched only Amazon. The BBC says its test was not a rigorous scientific study.

segments.title: Check the price at the source
segments.body: A consumer group quoted by the BBC warns that inaccurate prices can waste shoppers’ time or hide products that are actually within budget. A specialist in how products appear in AI results also cautions that recommendations may reflect stale prices or retailer visibility. The practical advice: check the retailer’s listing and do not treat an AI answer as a verified deal.

content.headline: London’s AI safety community grows, but faces access and energy limits
content.shortHeadline: London’s AI safety hub faces hurdles beyond research
content.standfirst: London hosts researchers, regulators and campaigners working on AI risks, including cyber misuse and biological threats. Their influence depends in part on access to leading models and on infrastructure constrained by the city’s energy supply.

image.caption: King’s Cross, home to a growing cluster of AI safety organisations.

sources.originalTitle: London's urgent race to make AI safer

segments.body: The BBC reports that as many as 50 organisations in London focus on AI safety, including the UK AI Security Institute, which assesses risks from leading models, and groups studying whether systems could act against human interests. The city is also home to AI companies and research efforts at the intersection of AI and biology.

segments.title: The limits of influence
segments.body: Researchers quoted by the BBC say independent scrutiny is difficult when access to cutting-edge models before release is limited. London’s growth also depends on data centres, while a report for the Greater London Authority identifies energy as the most critical constraint on their expansion. The city’s safety ambitions therefore rely on both access to technology and the infrastructure to support it.

content.headline: Trump threatens a tax on US firms building AI data centres abroad
content.shortHeadline: Trump threatens tax on US firms building data centres abroad
content.standfirst: The president floated a “tremendous tax” on companies building data centres outside the US, but gave no details and said he had not discussed the idea with his team. The threat comes as local opposition and restrictions complicate construction at home.

sources.originalTitle: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas

segments.body: Donald Trump said US companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they built data centres in other countries, arguing that the US must keep AI infrastructure at home to avoid falling behind China. He offered no details on how the proposal would work and said he had not raised it with his team before announcing it publicly.

segments.title: A policy idea, not a settled plan
segments.body: The BBC and The Verge report that major technology firms have projects or agreements overseas, and that the practical reach of such a policy remains unclear. The threat comes as communities and some state and local governments push back against data-centre construction in the US, potentially increasing companies’ interest in other locations.

content.headline: Man Utd’s manager costs near £100m as Berrada defends the club hierarchy
content.shortHeadline: Man Utd’s manager costs near £100m as Berrada defends the club
content.standfirst: A new filing puts Manchester United’s hiring and firing bill since 2013 at £95m, before further costs are added. Chief executive Omar Berrada has also defended the club’s summer recruitment amid supporter criticism.

image.caption: Mauricio Pochettino held his first Manchester United news conference.

sources.originalTitle: Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears £100m
Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada

segments.body:
Manchester United say they owe US Soccer £7.5m in compensation for Mauricio Pochettino’s release from his USA deal. That takes the club’s manager hiring and firing costs since Sir Alex Ferguson retired to £95m, a figure expected to pass £100m once the cost of Pochettino’s staff and Michael Carrick’s dismissal are included.

The club borrowed another £10m on 16 November, three days after announcing Pochettino. Its filing also shows £240m owed on its rolling credit limit and £417m in outstanding transfer fees, including £181m due after a year.

segments.title: Criticism and recruitment
segments.body: Berrada said he understood supporters’ frustration at United sitting 18th, and accepted that some criticism was fair, but said some had “crossed a line”. He defended the club’s summer signings, while acknowledging that it could have added a defender if the right player and value had been available.

perspectives.body: Berrada says United are happy with their summer recruitment and will not spend simply to silence critics. Pochettino, meanwhile, said he wants to be involved in the main decisions about the squad.

content.headline: England’s revival faces its toughest test yet against New Zealand
content.shortHeadline: England’s revival faces a major test against New Zealand
content.standfirst: After scoring 20 tries in wins over Australia and Japan, England meet an All Blacks side stung by a first defeat by Wales in 73 years. The contest will test whether England’s improved depth and attacking form can stand up to elite opposition.

image.caption: England beat Japan 78-15 last weekend.

sources.originalTitle: Stacked England aim to pile on style and add to All Black misery

segments.body: England’s emphatic recent wins have restored some confidence after five straight defeats earlier in the year. Their attack has produced 20 tries against Australia and Japan, but New Zealand are a substantially sterner test: the All Blacks have lost four of their past seven matches and arrive after their historic defeat by Wales.

segments.title: Depth back in the picture
segments.body: England have regained several players from injury, including full-back George Furbank and prop Will Stuart, while the bench offers further options such as Marcus Smith and Henry Pollock. They are still without Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Tom Curry and Alex Mitchell, but coach Steve Borthwick says the squad’s depth is back to a level last seen a year ago.

content.headline: Cricket Australia backs Cummins as captain amid renewed sandpaper claims
content.shortHeadline: Cricket Australia backs Cummins amid renewed sandpaper claims
content.standfirst: Cricket Australia will continue to support Pat Cummins as Test captain as new accounts reopen the 2018 ball-tampering dispute. Cummins denies knowing about the plan; fast bowler Josh Hazlewood says he would consider leaving if Cummins were forced out.

image.caption: Pat Cummins, who was named Australia captain in 2021.

sources.originalTitle: Cummins retains Cricket Australia support as captain

segments.body: Cricket Australia is backing Cummins to remain captain, a role he has held since 2021, despite renewed allegations over the 2018 Cape Town Test. Cameron Bancroft’s recent account supported earlier claims by Usman Khawaja that the whole team knew about the plan to tamper with the ball. Cummins has denied involvement or knowledge and called Khawaja’s claims “100% wrong”.

segments.title: Backing from a team-mate
segments.body: Hazlewood, who played in the Cape Town Test, said he would consider quitting the team if Cummins were made to stand down. Bancroft has also alleged that players and coaches celebrated when the ball-tampering succeeded; those claims remain contested.

perspectives.body: Hazlewood called the recent criticism a “pile on” and said he wanted to back Cummins. His comments underline that the dispute could affect the current team as well as revisiting the 2018 scandal.

content.headline: Alcaraz reaches ATP Finals semi-finals with perfect group record
content.shortHeadline: Alcaraz reaches ATP Finals semis despite injury concerns
content.standfirst: Carlos Alcaraz beat Flavio Cobolli in straight sets to complete the group stage without defeat, despite a hamstring problem. He next faces Ben Shelton, while Daniil Medvedev meets Alexander Zverev in the other semi-final.

image.caption: Carlos Alcaraz is seeking his first ATP Finals title.

sources.originalTitle: Alcaraz puts aside injury concerns to take apart Cobolli

segments.body:
Alcaraz, wearing strapping on his left leg after hurting his hamstring against Daniil Medvedev, beat Flavio Cobolli 6-4 6-1 in 65 minutes. He did not face a break point and hit 29 winners, extending his winning run to 12 matches.

The Spaniard said the immediate challenge was recovering physically for the next day’s semi-final against Ben Shelton. Alcaraz has never won the season-ending title.

content.headline: Kim takes three-shot LPGA lead after hole-in-one; Hull stays in contention
content.shortHeadline: Kim leads LPGA finale by three; Hull remains in the mix
content.standfirst: A-Lim Kim’s hole-in-one helped her shoot 64 and move to 15 under at the CME Group Tour Championship. Charley Hull is four strokes back after a bogey-free 67, with the tournament’s $4m top prize still in play.

image.caption: A-Lim Kim, whose only major title came at the 2020 US Women’s Open.

sources.originalTitle: Kim moves clear at LPGA finale after hole-in-one

segments.body:
Kim made a hole-in-one at the par-three 16th on her way to a seven-under 64, taking the outright lead at 15 under after two rounds. Jeeno Thitikul is second on 12 under.

England’s Charley Hull is among six players tied for third at 11 under after a bogey-free 67. The tournament’s $4m top prize is at stake on Sunday.

content.headline: Mudryk rejects Shevchenko’s account as dispute over drugs test escalates
content.shortHeadline: Mudryk rejects Shevchenko’s account of drugs-test dispute
content.standfirst: Mykhailo Mudryk says Andriy Shevchenko is lying about whether the winger asked a Ukrainian football official to take blame for his positive test. Mudryk repeats his allegations against the association and says he has evidence, which it has not yet responded to in the report.

image.caption: Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: Shevchenko lying about drugs test claims - Mudryk

segments.body:
Mudryk has denied Shevchenko’s accusation that his representatives repeatedly asked a Ukrainian Association of Football employee to take the blame for his meldonium test. In a statement, the winger called that account a “lie” and said neither he nor his representatives made such a request.

Mudryk, who was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026, says he believes the substance entered his system while on international duty. He also accuses the association of withholding information and misleading his team, and says WhatsApp messages support his claim that he used its supplements at training camps.

content.headline: Ireland and South Africa meet amid suspensions and a charged build-up
content.shortHeadline: Ireland and South Africa meet amid disciplinary tensions
content.standfirst: South Africa face Ireland in Dublin without banned coach Rassie Erasmus, while both teams have had late changes to their squads. Ireland are looking to respond to a run of heavy defeats against leading sides.

image.caption: Siya Kolisi spoke about what rugby means to people in South Africa.

sources.originalTitle: 'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without Erasmus

segments.body:
Erasmus will miss the match after receiving a six-match ban for questioning officials following South Africa’s defeat by France. Assistant coach Mzwandile Stick backed him, while Ireland captain Dan Sheehan said the suspension had no effect on his team.

South Africa back-row Jasper Wiese is also suspended. Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast was cleared to play after being cited over an alleged hip-drop tackle.

segments.title: A test for Ireland
segments.body: Ireland have lost their past six matches against New Zealand, France and South Africa by double-digit margins. Sheehan, usually a hooker, will captain from number eight with several back-row players unavailable. South Africa have brought in Franco Mostert after Ruan Nortje was ruled out through injury.

perspectives.body: Stick says South Africa’s players remain united behind Erasmus. Ireland’s Sheehan, by contrast, said the disciplinary story has “zero impact” on his side’s preparation.

content.headline: Kulusevski and Everton captain Finnigan describe the toll of long injuries
content.shortHeadline: Kulusevski and Finnigan on the isolation of long injuries
content.standfirst: Dejan Kulusevski and Everton’s Megan Finnigan describe loneliness, doubts and the strain of lengthy rehabilitation. Both have returned to action after serious injuries kept them out for more than a season.

image.caption: Dejan Kulusevski has been working towards a return after a long injury absence.

sources.originalTitle: Loneliness & mood swings - what's it like to miss a season through injury?

segments.body: Tottenham’s Kulusevski says he wondered whether he could play again after a serious knee injury kept him out for 18 months and cost him a place at the 2026 World Cup. He returned as a substitute in October after 526 days away and says he no longer takes playing for granted.

segments.title: The mental toll
segments.body: Everton captain Finnigan says she lost her confidence and “sparkle” during 602 days out with a cruciate ligament injury. Former England midfielder Fara Williams also highlights the financial pressure some women face while injured, including bills and uncertainty over short-term contracts.
